summary: An overview for new Internet users, answering commonly asked questions in a consumer-friendly way. It is informational and replaced RFC 1594.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo is a question and answer sheet for people who are new to the Internet. It explains in everyday language what the Internet is, what the addresses in an e-mail or a web link mean, how a message travels across it, and how to stay safe while using it.

subtitle: A plain-language question and answer sheet that explains the Internet to ordinary new users.

tldr.problem: New, non-technical Internet users kept asking the same basic questions, and earlier guides were aimed at more technical readers.
tldr.mechanism: The memo answers them in plain language: what the Internet is, what you can do on it, what addresses mean, how it works, who runs it and how to stay safe.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 1594 as FYI 4 and points readers who want more depth to FYI 7.

today: RFC 2664 is an Informational memo, FYI 4, that obsoletes RFC 1594, and no later RFC is listed as replacing it. It is a 1999 snapshot written for consumers of that era.

sections.title: Who This Guide Is For
sections.content:
The memo gives an overview for the new Internet user. Its intended audience is the common Internet user of today, so it takes a consumer-oriented approach rather than going into depth on any topic. Unlike its predecessors, this edition seeks to answer the general questions an unsophisticated consumer would ask, rather than the more pointed questions of a technically sophisticated user. Those wanting a more in-depth discussion are directed to FYI 7, which deals with intermediate and advanced question and answer topics. A conscious effort was made to keep the memo brief while still giving a new user enough information to generally understand the Internet.

The authors also record that the document was consumer tested in South Riding, Virginia, by two people, and they thank Chris Burke of Motorola, John Curran of BBN Planet, Albert Lunde of Northwestern University and April Marine of Internet Engines, along with the acknowledgements to Patricia Harper and Charlotte Nurge.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says plainly who it is for: ordinary people using the Internet, not network engineers. It keeps the answers short and points readers who want more to a companion document, FYI 7.

sections.title: What the Internet Is and What People Do on It
sections.content:
People use computers to perform a wide assortment of tasks, and a connected group of computers is known as a network. Some computers are connected directly to the network, while others, primarily those in homes, are connected via a telephone line and a communication device known as a modem. By connecting networks together with specialized computers known as routers, people on one network can engage in activities with people on other networks. This interconnected group of networks is known as the Internet.

The memo then lists what people do on the Internet: surfing, searching, sending mail, transferring programs and documents, chatting and playing games. Surfing uses a web browser to reach a location that contains information, and the links between locations are usually underlined text in a different colour, so clicking one takes the reader to that information, which may be at the same location or a different one, and which may itself contain more links. Searching uses a search engine at a search site, and the popular browsers hold the locations of these sites; the memo compares this to a card catalog in a library, where a topic is looked up and a list of references with locations is found.

E-mail is compared to sending letters through the post office, and the memo notes that because it can be misunderstood or abused, users should be familiar with email netiquette. Many people also take part in mailing lists, which are usually dedicated to a particular topic or interest and are used either to pass on information or to hold a discussion, in which case people send mail to a list address and it is distributed to all members. The memo says abuse of mail lists is probably the biggest source of junk mail, also known as spam, and that everyone should take care not to be the source of junk mail. Programs and documents are transferred by attaching them to an e-mail message, or from sites to users with the save feature of a web browser or the file transfer protocol. Chat takes place in chat rooms, which are generally sponsored or operated by an organization with an interest in the topic, and the memo warns first-time users that some people only listen and that some may portray themselves as someone different from who they really are. Games may be role-playing games, action games or online versions of older standbys such as chess, and other popular activities include electronic shopping, banking and investing, with a word of caution to check that a reputable site says how it protects credit card information, and to avoid using a credit card at a site if in doubt.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet is simply a set of networks joined together. Once you are on it you can read pages, search for information, send mail, download files, talk to other people and play games. The memo compares searching to a library card catalog and chatting to a party where some people only listen.

sections.title: E-mail Addresses and Web Addresses
sections.content:
Two commonly asked questions are what your e-mail address is and what the URL is. Generally, the first question asks where to send information and the second asks where to get information. The answer to the first is usually something like myname@company.com, pronounced as the name at the company dot com, and the answer to the second is usually something like http://www.newspaper.com.

An e-mail address consists of two parts divided by an at sign. The portion to the left is like the name line on a letter: it identifies a particular person and is usually composed of the person's name, with typical names such as john_doe, john.doe, jdoe or doej. That name is assigned by the system or network administrator who manages the e-mail system and follows rules established by the company providing the e-mail service, and it is sometimes called a mailbox. The portion to the right of the at sign is the name of the computer system providing the e-mail service, usually the name of the company that owns the system, followed by a dot and an abbreviation for the domain or group of names the organisation falls under. Examples of these top-level domains are edu and com, and country codes such as fr for France and jp for Japan. When an e-mail is sent, the portion to the right of the at sign is used to find the destination computer.

A Uniform Resource Locator is commonly used to identify a computer that provides World Wide Web service. It also has two parts, this time separated by the double slash. The portion to the left means find the World Wide Web service located at the computer identified to the right of the double slash, and the portion to the right is the name of the computer providing that service, composed of parts similar to those used for the name of an e-mail computer. Sometimes the right portion also carries extra information identifying a particular document at the site, so http://www.newspaper.com/sports/article1.html identifies a specific article in the sports section of the newspaper.
sections.plainLanguage: An e-mail address says who should receive the message and which computer system handles it. A URL says which computer to go to for information, and can also point at one particular document on that computer.

sections.title: Rules of Behavior on the Internet
sections.content:
In general, common sense, courtesy and decency govern good Internet behavior, and there is no single formal rulebook. FYI 28 is offered as a good guide, and many activities such as game sites, chat rooms or e-mail lists have rules of their own, so what is acceptable in one chat room may be out of bounds in another. The memo advises users to check the water temperature before jumping in the pool and to take the same precautions before joining any online activity.

E-mail in particular can lead to misunderstandings between people, because the reader has only the text to work out what is being said; other cues such as tone of voice and body signals like winking are not present in the text. Users have therefore developed cues to put in the text, using techniques such as capitalization and symbols known as emoticons, or smilies, of which a typical smiley looks like :). Acronyms have also evolved over time, the memo giving IMHO, in my humble opinion, as an example, and it suggests searching with keywords such as netiquette and emoticon to find more information.

Users should also be aware that their programs, such as word processors or e-mail clients, may produce documents and messages that are not readable by everyone, since a reader often needs the same program in which the document was written. Before sending an attached document it is therefore a good idea to check that the intended receiver can read it, and if in doubt to send a plain text version.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no rulebook for the Internet, so the same manners you would use in person apply. Because a message has no tone of voice, people have invented shortcuts such as capital letters and smiley faces to show how they feel.

sections.title: How the Internet Carries a Message, and Who Runs It
sections.content:
Every activity described in the memo needs computers to exchange information, and computers take turns sending and receiving. A computer sending information is the source, and one receiving it is the destination; the same computer can be both at different times, which is clear when thinking of sending and receiving e-mail. Every computer has a unique Internet address that identifies it from among the millions of computers, and the Internet has specialized computers between the source and destination at network interconnection points, known as routers, which use a computer's address to point information from one computer to another.

The memo lists what happens in an exchange of information. The source finds the address of the destination and contacts it, saying hello; the destination answers with a hello of its own. The source says it has information to send and the destination says it is ready to receive. The source breaks the information into small pieces called packets and sends each packet on its way, the routers guide each packet to the destination, and the destination puts the packets back together to form the information. The destination then says it has received the information and asks whether the source has anything more to send. If the source says no, the destination says goodbye unless it has something to send back, in which case it breaks that information into packets and sends them, and once both end users are done talking they both say goodbye.

The memo admits that this simplified account leaves out many steps, such as how a computer discovers the address of another computer or how packets are divided and reassembled, and adds that these are specifics that people using the Internet never really need to deal with.

As for who runs the Internet, the answer given is nobody. The Internet is a cooperative effort among Internet service providers, software companies, volunteer organizations and a few facilities that tie the whole thing together. The providers and software companies are independent of each other and most of them compete with each other. The providers give people Internet service much as people obtain telephone service from a telephone company, and they agree to connect their networks to each other and to pass information following an established set of rules, the protocols. The software companies agree to make programs such as e-mail clients and web browsers that follow the same protocols. Other organizations keep things straight: some assign Internet addresses much as telephone numbers are assigned, others keep track of the names used by Internet users and groups, and a large volunteer organization called the Internet Engineering Task Force develops the protocols that computers follow to make network communications succeed.
sections.plainLanguage: A message is cut into small pieces called packets, and routers carry each packet to its destination, which puts the pieces back together. Nobody owns the Internet: providers, software makers and volunteer organizations agree on the rules and keep them working.

sections.title: Three Rules of Thumb for Safety
sections.content:
The question of whether the Internet is secure can be a confusing one, because people hear many assurances that it is secure and many scary stories saying that it is not. The memo gives a few basic rules of thumb that address most concerns.

First, make it a rule never to share account passwords with anyone. Learning a password is the easiest way for someone to break into a system. Most people feel that their files are not that interesting to anyone, but someone may get a foothold from one innocuous account to other places in the same computer system, and the memo points to the User's Security Handbook, FYI 34.

Second, understand that there are means for people to track the information a user sends by e-mail, the files one downloads and the sites visited on the web. System administrators and network engineers who oversee a site's computers require access to information that an individual may think is secret, and in practice no responsible administrator violates a person's privacy out of personal curiosity. However, if someone less legitimate attains illegal access to a system, they will also have access to that information. An e-mail sent a year ago, or a log of the web pages a user browsed, may still exist in a system's backup archive and can be resurrected and published widely.

Third, before giving personal information over the Internet, such as filling in a form on a web page, users should realize that there is no assurance of confidentiality or privacy. It could be compared to faxing such information to a party you have never dealt with before: while many organizations are responsible with information received by web and e-mail, that cannot always be determined in advance.
sections.plainLanguage: Three habits cover most of the worry: keep passwords to yourself, remember that what you send can be traced, and treat any form that asks for personal details with the caution you would apply to a stranger sending you a fax.

items.title: Never share passwords
items.text: Learning a password is the easiest way for someone to break into a system, and one account can lead to others on the same computer.

items.text: E-mail, downloaded files and the sites visited can be seen by administrators, and old copies may still exist in backup archives.

items.text: Before giving personal information over the Internet, remember there is no assurance of confidentiality or privacy.
